items.title: NEW: Virginia Tech Provost/Cranwell issue formal guidance on the D/S rule -- Aug 31, 2026 deadline for grad program/major changes and school transfers
items.source: Virginia Tech News / Office of the Executive Vice President and Provost + Cranwell International Center (official university notice)
items.summary: Virginia Tech's Office of the Provost and the Cranwell International Center (CIC) published formal guidance for VT faculty and staff on anticipated campus impacts of the Sep 15, 2026 DHS Duration-of-Status final rule (see item 'd-s-final-rule'). Key points directly relevant to a student who may need an extra semester: (1) all F-1/J-1 students will face increased external (USCIS-level) review of timely progress toward a degree, with any program extension now going through what VT describes as a more heavily monitored extension process; (2) students who complete one program after Sep 15, 2026 are barred from starting another program at the same or a lower level (e.g., master's-to-master's is out; master's-to-PhD remains allowed), matching the federal rule; (3) graduate students will be unable to transfer institutions or change programs until their current degree is completed; (4) undergraduates will be unable to transfer schools or change their declared major during their first year of study. Most actionable for students right now: Cranwell has set a hard internal deadline of Monday, Aug 31, 2026 for all paperwork requesting a program/major change, a program-level change (e.g., PhD to master's), or a school transfer -- submissions, including advisor comments, must reach CIC by that date to be processed under the current (pre-Sep-15) rules; this can run concurrently with the Graduate School's own approval process. This is the first Virginia-Tech-specific implementation guidance found since the D/S final rule was published on Jul 17, 2026; Cranwell's general 'Duration of Status Updates' page had previously said only that the university was still reviewing impacts with no VT-specific procedural guidance. New detail found today (2026-08-23), from Cranwell's own Duration of Status Updates page: extension requests are not reviewed until after the first day of classes in a student's final term, regardless of the reason for the request, and Cranwell states it will only be reviewing extension requests for students with a Fall 2026 program end date (Fall 2026 classes end Wed, Dec 9, 2026; degree conferral Wed, Dec 16, 2026) -- a student whose program end date falls later (e.g. Spring 2027 or beyond) is not yet described as eligible to have an extension request reviewed under this guidance. New today (2026-08-25): Cranwell is holding mandatory 'D/S Basics' webinars for all F-1/J-1 advisees on Tue, Aug 25, 2026, 7:00 PM ET (today) and Fri, Aug 28, 2026, 9:00 AM ET, ahead of the Aug 31, 2026 paperwork deadline and the Sep 15, 2026 rule effective date.
items.notes: Second check, 2026-08-23: re-read international.vt.edu/duration_of_status.html directly and found two additional operational details not captured in yesterday's first pass -- (1) Cranwell will not review any extension request, regardless of reason, until after the first day of classes in the student's final term; (2) as of today, Cranwell states it is only reviewing extension requests for students whose program end date falls in Fall 2026. This second point is the single most directly actionable fact this tracker has found for a student wondering whether Cranwell can act on an extra-semester request right now: if your program end date is NOT Fall 2026, this guidance does not describe your extension request as currently being reviewed. The Aug 31, 2026 paperwork deadline for program/major changes and school transfers is unchanged. Will keep monitoring for whether Cranwell extends review to later program end dates (e.g. Spring 2027) as the Sep 15 transition nears. Third check, 2026-08-24: no changes found -- Cranwell's Duration of Status Updates page still describes the same Fall-2026-only extension review window and the Aug 31, 2026 paperwork deadline for program/major changes and school transfers, which is now exactly one week away. Twelfth check, 2026-08-25: Cranwell's Immigration Updates page now lists two mandatory 'D/S Basics' webinar sessions for F-1/J-1 advisees -- today, Tue Aug 25, 2026 at 7:00 PM ET, and Fri Aug 28, 2026 at 9:00 AM ET. The Aug 31, 2026 paperwork deadline for program/major changes and school transfers is unchanged and now only a few days away. No change to the Fall-2026-only extension review window.

items.title: DHS Final Rule: Fixed Time Period of Admission & Extension of Stay (ends Duration of Status) for F, J, I nonimmigrants
items.summary: DHS published a final rule (doc. 2026-14439) on Jul 17, 2026, ending open-ended Duration of Status for F-1 students, effective Sep 15, 2026. Students get a fixed 'Admit Until Date' capped at 4 years (24 months for language programs); anyone needing more time must file Form I-539 (Extension of Stay) with USCIS in addition to the existing DSO SEVIS extension -- the I-539 EOS filing fee is reported as $420 filed online / $470 by paper. A timely-filed EOS gives up to 240 days of authorized stay while pending. The rule also shortens the F-1 post-completion grace period from 60 to 30 days for anyone who travels/re-enters or gets an EOS approval after the effective date. Students already in D/S status who remain continuously in the U.S. without leaving/re-entering keep transition protections, but only up to a hard outside cap of Nov 14, 2030 (4 years + 60-day grace period measured from the Sep 15, 2026 effective date). DHS has discretion to postpone, until as late as Sep 14, 2028, implementation of the specific provisions restricting mid-program school transfers, changes in educational objective (major/level), and progression to same- or lower-level programs, if DHS determines full implementation isn't feasible by the Sep 15, 2026 effective date -- this discretionary postponement option applies only to those specific transfer/education-level provisions, not to the core fixed-admission-period change itself. As a major rule, it is also subject to Congressional Review Act review: Congress has a 60-day window after the rule is reported to introduce a joint resolution of disapproval, which -- if enacted -- would void the rule and bar a substantially similar rule absent new legislation; as of this run no such resolution has been reported as introduced. USCIS will publish revised editions of Form I-539 and Form I-765 effective Sep 15, 2026, aligned to the new fixed-admission-period process -- the current 08/28/24 edition of Form I-539 will still be accepted if postmarked or e-filed before Sep 15, 2026, but rejected on/after that date (no grace period), after which only the new 09/15/26 edition is accepted. On Aug 18, 2026, the anticipated legal challenge became a real lawsuit: NAFSA, the Presidents' Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration, and other higher-ed/labor groups filed a complaint and motion for preliminary injunction against the rule in the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts (case assigned to District Judge F. Dennis Saylor, IV), seeking to stay and vacate it (or at minimum block its enforcement against plaintiffs and their members) before the Sep 15, 2026 effective date -- see item 'lawsuit-vs-ds-rule-2026-08' for full details. SEVP is hosting a live stakeholder webinar on Mon, Aug 31, 2026, 2-3pm ET to review the rule's major changes and answer FAQs. Virginia Tech's Office of the Provost and Cranwell International Center have now published VT-specific implementation guidance -- see the new item 'vt-provost-cic-guidance-2026-08' -- including a hard Aug 31, 2026 deadline for graduate students needing a program/major change or school transfer processed before the transition.
items.notes: Update 2026-08-22 (ninth check): no ruling yet on the preliminary injunction motion (see 'lawsuit-vs-ds-rule-2026-08'); the case is now confirmed assigned to District Judge F. Dennis Saylor, IV in D. Mass. No Congressional Review Act disapproval resolution has been introduced as of this run -- a targeted congress.gov search today found only an unrelated DHS H-1B/F-1 disapproval resolution (H.J.Res.22, targeting a December 2024 rule), not this rule. No new form-specific e-filing mandate notice for I-539/I-765 has been published (see 'uscis-mandatory-efiling-rule-2026'). SEVP stakeholder webinar remains scheduled for Mon, Aug 31, 2026, 2-3pm ET per Study in the States. Biggest development today: Virginia Tech's Office of the Provost and Cranwell International Center published dedicated VT-specific implementation guidance for the first time (see new item 'vt-provost-cic-guidance-2026-08'), including a hard Aug 31, 2026 paperwork deadline for graduate students needing a program/major change or school transfer. Update 2026-08-23 (tenth check): no ruling yet on the preliminary injunction motion (see 'lawsuit-vs-ds-rule-2026-08', which today obtained the case's exact docket number). No new CRA disapproval resolution found. SEVP's Aug 31, 2026 stakeholder webinar (2-3pm ET) is confirmed as requiring no advance registration -- just log on -- with attendance capped at 1,000 participants; a recording and transcript will be posted afterward. No new form-specific I-539/I-765 e-filing mandate notice found. Update 2026-08-24 (eleventh check): no ruling yet on the preliminary injunction motion. No new CRA disapproval resolution found. SEVP's Aug 31, 2026 stakeholder webinar remains scheduled as previously described. No new form-specific I-539/I-765 e-filing mandate notice found. Sep 15, 2026 effective date remains on track pending court action. Update 2026-08-25 (twelfth check): confirmed directly via a USCIS newsroom alert that revised editions of Form I-539 and Form I-765 publish Sep 15, 2026 with no grace period -- the 08/28/24 I-539 edition is rejected if postmarked/e-filed on/after Sep 15, 2026, and only the new 09/15/26 edition is accepted from that date forward. Secondary reporting (not yet independently verified against a primary USCIS source) adds that F-1/J-1 students admitted under D/S who timely file post-completion OPT or STEM OPT applications on or before Mar 18, 2027 are reported as not required to separately file Form I-539 for that OPT/STEM OPT period -- flagging this for continued verification rather than treating it as confirmed. items.title: Coalition sues DHS, seeks preliminary injunction to block/vacate the D/S-ending final rule before Sep 15
items.source: Presidents' Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration / NAFSA (press release); press reporting
items.summary: On Aug 18, 2026, a coalition -- NAFSA: Association of International Educators, the Presidents' Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration, the Association of Independent Colleges and Universities in Massachusetts (AICUM), the American Federation of Teachers (AFT), the Graduate Labor Organization (AFT Local 6516), the UAW, UAW Local 2322, and The NewsGuild-CWA -- filed a complaint and motion for preliminary injunction in the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts challenging DHS's July 17, 2026 final rule that ends Duration of Status for F, J, and I nonimmigrants. Plaintiffs, represented by law firm McDermott Will & Schulte per Inside Higher Ed's reporting, argue the rule violates the Administrative Procedure Act -- that DHS failed to adequately assess the rule's costs and benefits, meaningfully respond to public comments, consider less burdensome alternatives, or justify the rule based on its stated objectives, and that DHS also provided an inadequate public comment period and exceeded its statutory authority -- and ask the court to stay and vacate the rule, or at minimum enjoin its enforcement against plaintiffs and their members, before it takes effect Sep 15, 2026. The case has been assigned to District Judge F. Dennis Saylor, IV of the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts, and now carries a confirmed docket number: 1:26-cv-13799 (Presidents' Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration et al. v. U.S. Department of Homeland Security et al., D. Mass., filed Aug. 18, 2026). Legal commentary (Fragomen) notes that, given the timeline, employers and students should continue preparing for the Sep 15 effective date in case the emergency-stay request is not decided in time. Directly relevant to a student weighing an extra semester: if the court grants a stay or injunction before Sep 15, the fixed-admission-period/I-539 Extension-of-Stay requirement could be paused or delayed for some or all F-1 students; if the motion is denied or not decided in time, the rule proceeds as scheduled on Sep 15. The case is now independently confirmed via CourtListener's federal court docket record (PACER-sourced), docket 74661796, assigned to Judge F. Dennis Saylor IV, filed Aug 18, 2026, last known filing activity Aug 20, 2026. The court set an expedited briefing schedule: DHS's response is due Aug 31, 2026, with a motion hearing expected in early September 2026 -- both dates land just before the rule's Sep 15, 2026 effective date.
items.notes: First identified 2026-08-19 via multiple simultaneous press reports, corroborated by the plaintiff coalition's own press release. Update 2026-08-20 (second check): Inside Higher Ed and NAFSA added dedicated coverage/press-release pages. Update 2026-08-21 (third check): two more organizations -- the Presidents' Alliance and EnglishUSA -- now host dedicated 'Duration of Status Litigation' tracker/support pages; Fragomen's law-firm alert and Inside Higher Ed detail identify plaintiffs' counsel as McDermott Will & Schulte. Mass. filing in search results, so this remains 'Reported, unconfirmed' pending an official court-source confirmation. No ruling on the preliminary injunction motion yet as of this run. Update 2026-08-23 (fifth check): the exact docket number, 1:26-cv-13799, is now confirmed via multiple sources (Bloomberg Law, American Bazaar) and directly from the plaintiffs' own hosted copies of the as-filed Complaint and preliminary-injunction motion PDFs (Case 1:26-cv-13799, Document 1, filed 08/18/26). No ruling on the preliminary injunction motion has been reported yet. items.title: USCIS Interim Final Rule enabling mandatory electronic filing (e-Filing) -- covers I-539/I-765 among forms in scope
items.summary: USCIS published an interim final rule (91 FR 51924, doc. 2026-16313), effective Aug 11, 2026, giving USCIS authority to require mandatory electronic filing (e-filing) of certain benefit requests. The rule itself does not immediately force any specific form online -- USCIS may only mandate e-filing for a form once that form has been available for e-filing for at least 180 days, and must give at least 60 days' advance public notice before a mandate for a specific form/filing circumstance takes effect. It does not affect petitions already pending. Secondary coverage lists an initial set of roughly 22 forms USCIS is expected to phase toward mandatory e-filing, reportedly including I-129, I-130, N-400, I-90, I-131, and -- notably -- I-539 (Extension/Change of Nonimmigrant Status) and I-765 (Employment Authorization). This directly matters for F-1 students who will need to file Form I-539 for an Extension of Stay (EOS) once the Sep 15, 2026 fixed-admission-period rule takes effect, and for I-765 OPT/STEM OPT applicants: if/when USCIS issues the required 60-day notice mandating e-filing for these forms, paper filing could stop being accepted for them. Public comments on the interim final rule are open through Oct 13, 2026.
items.notes: First identified 2026-08-18 via a general OPT/CPT news sweep, then confirmed directly against the Federal Register document and a matching official USCIS newsroom alert ('USCIS To Require Electronic Filing of Forms: Strengthening National Security'). Rechecked 2026-08-19 through 2026-08-21 (second-fourth checks): still no 60-day mandate notice for any specific form (including I-539/I-765) had been published. Rechecked 2026-08-22 (fifth check): still no form-specific 60-day mandate notice published for I-539, I-765, or any of the ~22 forms in scope -- only the enabling interim final rule remains in effect. Comments remain open through Oct 13, 2026. Will keep tracking for the first form-specific mandate notice, which is the actionable trigger for students filing extension-of-stay or OPT paperwork. items.title: Reported $100,000 fee under consideration for OPT / post-completion work authorization
items.source: Press reporting (Forbes, Bloomberg, ICEF Monitor, The PIE News, Higher Ed Dive)
items.summary: Multiple outlets report the administration is weighing a $100,000 fee applicable to OPT employment authorization (and by extension STEM OPT), modeled on the now-struck-down $100,000 H-1B fee proclamation. As of this run, no signed proclamation or DHS proposed rule/fee schedule has been reported for an OPT fee -- unlike the H-1B fee, which was signed via proclamation on Sep 19, 2025 and then struck down by Judge Sorokin on Jun 8, 2026. Note: a SEPARATE H-1B petition-fee rule (RIN 1615-AD20) cleared White House/OIRA review on Aug 19, 2026 -- this is a distinct H-1B-specific rulemaking, not an OPT fee, and should not be conflated with the reported $100K OPT fee tracked in this item. Immigration attorneys quoted say an OPT fee is unlikely to survive legal challenge absent Congressional authorization, citing that H-1B precedent. Who would pay (student/university/employer) remains unresolved; USCIS has not published regulatory language explaining the proposal, coverage, exemptions, or administration. Directly relevant to students weighing an extra semester who are also counting on post-completion OPT/STEM OPT to work in the U.S. afterward. New development as of 2026-08-23 (per a Fragomen client alert): DHS's related H-1B petition-fee rule (RIN 1615-AD20, a separate rulemaking, tracked for context) cleared OMB/OIRA review on Aug 19, 2026, and a proposed OPT fee rule was itself submitted to OMB for review on Aug 20, 2026, and is now under review there. Fragomen notes the contents of both proposals remain confidential until released for publication in the Federal Register, and that neither proposal was included in DHS's most recent public regulatory agenda. This moves the OPT fee from informal press-reported deliberation into the formal OMB regulatory-review pipeline, but it is still not a published rule, RIN, or fee amount confirmed by DHS/USCIS -- the reported $100,000 figure itself remains unconfirmed by any official source.
items.notes: Still no DHS/USCIS/.gov statement, proposed rule, or signed proclamation found confirming or denying an OPT-specific fee as of 2026-08-22 (ninth check). Today's searches turned up a distinct, confirmed development -- a separate H-1B petition-fee rule (RIN 1615-AD20) cleared OIRA/White House review on Aug 19, 2026 -- but this is not the OPT fee reported here; no reginfo.gov entry or RIN has been found specifically for an OPT fee. No proclamation has been signed for OPT. Reporting continues to cite the struck-down H-1B fee precedent as the key legal headwind. Update 2026-08-23 (tenth check): Fragomen reports DHS submitted a proposed OPT fee rule to OMB for review on Aug 20, 2026 -- a real procedural step, though contents remain confidential pending Federal Register publication and no RIN specific to an OPT fee has been found on reginfo.gov. Still no signed proclamation, published NPRM, or confirmed fee amount from any .gov source. Update 2026-08-24 (eleventh check): a targeted site:reginfo.gov search for an OPT-specific RIN again returned no match. No signed proclamation, published NPRM, or confirmed fee amount from any .gov source as of today. Update 2026-08-25 (twelfth check): targeted site:reginfo.gov and site:whitehouse.gov searches for an OPT-specific RIN/OIRA entry again returned no match. Still no signed proclamation, published NPRM, or confirmed fee amount from any .gov source.

items.title: ICE/HSI announces nationwide OPT fraud crackdown: 10,000+ students linked to 'suspect employers'
items.source: Press reporting of ICE/HSI press conference (Acting Director Todd Lyons)
items.summary: At a May 12, 2026 press conference, Acting ICE Director Todd Lyons and Acting HSI Associate Director John Condon announced that federal investigators had identified more than 10,000 F-1/STEM OPT students linked to 'highly suspect employers' -- among the top 25 OPT-employing companies reviewed. HSI site visits across eight states (TX, VA, GA, IL, NY, NJ, NC, FL) reportedly found empty buildings, locked doors, residential addresses listed as worksites, shell companies, and offshore payroll/HR arrangements; in one Northern Texas case an employer claimed 500 OPT students but had only 3 actual employees on site. Lyons called it 'only the tip of the iceberg.' Directly relevant to any student counting on post-completion OPT/STEM OPT -- especially under an extended timeline -- since it signals intensified employer-level scrutiny and potential SEVIS/EAD complications for students whose employer gets flagged, even if the student did nothing wrong. The core claim is now independently confirmed: the DHS final rule's own preamble (doc. 2026-14439, Federal Register, Jul 17, 2026) cites Acting ICE Director Todd Lyons' May 12, 2026 press-conference statement that ICE 'identified more than 10,000 cases of potential fraud associated with the OPT program,' tying it directly to the rule's stated justification.
items.notes: Still widely reported by many independent outlets describing the same May 12, 2026 press conference. Rechecked 2026-08-20 through 2026-08-22 (seventh-ninth checks): targeted site:ice.gov / site:dhs.gov searches again surfaced only older/general SEVP fraud material (Operation OPTical Illusion 15-arrests release, a STEM OPT employer-fraud broadcast message, the Northern Virginia site-visit release) -- none matching the specific '10,000+ students' / May 12, 2026 press-conference claim. Both domains remain reachable and return other current, relevant SEVP material, so this continues to look like a genuine gap in official coverage of this specific number rather than a source-access problem. Rechecked 2026-08-23 (tenth check): targeted site:ice.gov / site:dhs.gov search again surfaced only the same older/general SEVP fraud material (STEM OPT employer-fraud broadcast message, Operation OPTical Illusion 15-arrests release, Northern Virginia site-visit release) -- still no official match for the specific '10,000+ students' / May 12, 2026 press-conference claim. Rechecked 2026-08-24 (eleventh check): same result -- targeted site:ice.gov / site:dhs.gov search surfaced only the same older/general SEVP fraud material, still no official match for the specific claim. Update 2026-08-25 (twelfth check, UPGRADED TO CONFIRMED): a targeted search found the specific '10,000+' figure quoted directly in the Federal Register final rule document (2026-14439) itself, in the section responding to public comments -- the rule cites Lyons' May 12, 2026 statement verbatim as part of its justification for ending D/S. Since this is now sourced to an official Federal Register document rather than only press accounts of the press conference, this item moves from 'Reported, unconfirmed' to 'Confirmed (official)'.

items.title: USCIS Policy Alert PA-2026-05: officers may deny incomplete filings without issuing an RFE/NOID first
items.summary: Effective Aug 5, 2026, USCIS updated Policy Manual guidance so adjudicators may, at their discretion, deny a benefit request lacking required initial evidence or failing to establish eligibility without first issuing an RFE or NOID, and may set RFE response deadlines shorter than the prior 12-week norm (the 14-day international-mail grace period was also eliminated). Directly relevant to F-1 students filing Form I-539 (Extension of Stay) or I-765 under the new fixed-admission-period regime: an incomplete EOS package can now be denied outright with no chance to cure. This compounds with the new mandatory e-filing framework (see item above), since incomplete or improperly formatted e-filed packages would carry the same denial risk.
items.notes: No changes found today (ninth check). Confirmed via the official USCIS newsroom alert and Policy Alert PA-2026-05, effective for requests pending/filed on/after Aug 5, 2026. No changes found today (tenth check). No changes found today (eleventh check, 2026-08-24). No changes found today (twelfth check, 2026-08-25).

items.title: SEVP Broadcast Message BCM 2608-01: DSOs warned on CPT authorization liability, increased scrutiny
items.summary: On Aug 12, 2026, SEVP issued Broadcast Message 2608-01, 'Reminder of Liability for DSOs Regarding CPT Authorization,' to every PDSO/DSO at SEVP-certified schools. SEVP says it has observed a rise in Curricular Practical Training (CPT) authorizations that do not meet regulatory requirements -- specifically CPT not constituting an integral part of an established curriculum -- and is increasing scrutiny of CPT approvals; the message states DSOs should only authorize CPT where its absence 'would make the attainment of a degree an impossibility.' The message does not change the CPT regulation itself and DHS's July D/S final rule separately stated it 'does not prohibit or eliminate Day-1 CPT' and 'does not make substantive changes to CPT.' But it signals stepped-up enforcement: schools found authorizing CPT improperly risk investigation and loss of SEVP certification. Washington State University's Aug 7, 2026 international-office advisory announced ISSS there will stop approving full-time CPT during the academic year starting Spring 2027, except for programs with an explicit mandatory-internship curriculum requirement -- an early example of a university preemptively tightening its own CPT approval practices. No indication yet that Virginia Tech's Cranwell International Center has announced a similar CPT-specific change; VT's CPT page still describes standard part-time/full-time CPT eligibility rules with no dated policy update, though VT's new provost/CIC guidance (see item 'vt-provost-cic-guidance-2026-08') does not mention CPT specifically either.
items.notes: No regulatory text has changed -- remains a compliance/enforcement reminder, not a rulemaking. items.title: 30 Senators press State Dept (Rubio) to clear F/M/J student visa interview backlog before fall term
items.source: Office of Sen. Alex Padilla (official press release) / press reporting
items.summary: On Aug 11, 2026, 30 U.S. Senators led by Sen. Alex Padilla sent a letter to Secretary of State Marco Rubio saying 'no timely visa appointments are available for students at some embassies and consulates' during peak season, and asking the State Department to restore priority to F, M, and J visa interviews, extend interview waivers for vetted returning students, and boost consular staffing before fall term starts. The letter poses 10 questions covering staffing, interview-slot allocation, and guidance sent to consular posts since August 2025, and gives State roughly 30 days to respond -- a written response is due around Sep 10, 2026, after most fall terms have already begun. Not a rule change, but directly relevant to any F-1 student (including someone on an extended timeline) who needs to obtain a new visa stamp or renew one to travel and re-enter, especially once the Sep 15, 2026 D/S-to-fixed-admission-period transition takes effect.
items.notes: No State Department response found yet (eighth check). Response remains pinned to ~Sep 10, 2026 (roughly 30 days from the Aug 11 letter), consistent with the prior run's estimate. items.title: NAFSA/JB International report: fall 2026 international enrollment projected to fall ~9.5% (~111,000-112,000 students) amid visa crackdown
items.source: NAFSA: Association of International Educators / JB International (research report, press reporting)
items.summary: A report released Aug 11, 2026 by NAFSA and research firm JB International, based on institutional responses to IIE's Spring 2026 Snapshot survey, projects fall 2026 international enrollment at U.S. colleges will fall about 9.5%, citing declining applications, visa-appointment bottlenecks, and newly restrictive immigration policy (including the D/S final rule) as converging headwinds. Inside Higher Ed's own writeup puts the projected total at roughly 1,057,000 international students enrolled in 2026-27, down from an estimated 1,169,000 in 2025-26 -- a loss of about 112,000 students, consistent with the ~111,000-112,000 range other outlets cite. Estimated economic impact: ~$3.4 billion in lost local spending and ~39,000-40,000 jobs. Inside Higher Ed's coverage adds that 63% of surveyed institutions anticipate an enrollment decline for 2026-2027 (vs. 11% expecting an increase, 26% expecting stable numbers). A CNBC report on Aug 21, 2026 corroborates the same downward enrollment trend citing tighter visa policy as a driver. This is a research/economic-impact projection rather than a new rule -- it is being tracked here as evidence of how seriously the sector expects the policy changes above to bite, which is relevant context (not itself an actionable status change) for a student weighing an extra semester.
items.notes: This remains a private-association economic/enrollment projection, not a government policy claim. Update 2026-08-22 (ninth check): a CNBC article (Aug 21, 2026) corroborates the same enrollment-decline trend and cites tighter visa policy, added as an additional secondary source; no change to the underlying estimate. NAFSA's own Fall 2026 Outlook document (nafsa.org/fall2026outlook) and JBI economic snapshot PDF remain the primary source for the underlying estimate. No material change today (tenth check).
